Fixed in src/distill-hardened.mjs by declaring IMG/CANVAS/VIDEO/SVG/PICTURE/EMBED/OBJECT with their rects (hit-tested, so occluded images are tagged too): the all-canvas page now yields '[pixels] canvas 0,0,1280,800' and the mixed page declares '[pixels] img 8,191,300,120'. Verified the duel numbers are unaffected: 0/20 duel pages contain any opaque element, and the post-fix re-run reproduces 1578 bytes / 391 tokens exactly.

measurements.notes: CROSS-WINDOW RESULT (the macOS analog of the Linux WM-map test, with a better ending): with TextEdit (z=12) over Chrome (z=14), the compositor map gives geometry + z-order, from which the back window computes as 25.3% covered. Per-window structure alone is blind to this — Chrome's own AX still reports the covered point as inside its frame. BUT macOS ships the mitigation as a first-class API: AXUIElementCopyElementAtPosition on the system-wide element, probed at a point inside the covered region, returns an AXTextArea belonging to pid 65570 = TextEdit — i.e. the FRONT window. So on macOS cross-window occlusion is resolved by ONE system call, with no rectangle math and no z-order bookkeeping, where the Linux cell had to compute overlap-vs-z-order by hand. Same primitive also solves in-window occlusion for native apps (no elementFromPoint equivalent needed).

runtime_verification.agreement: post-hardening the view matches what is visible, hittable AND pictorially opaque; every gap is now tagged ([occluded]) or declared ([pixels] rect). No silent case survived — but one had to be FOUND and FIXED first (t6).

measurements.notes: THE HEADLINE, AND IT DEFLATES THE SYNTHETIC RESULT: over 16 real sites the structured view costs 1360 tokens on average against 1366 for one CSS-resolution viewport screenshot. STATE THE AGGREGATION EXPLICITLY, because the two defensible summaries disagree and the difference is not cosmetic: the ratio of TOTALS (21766 structured tokens vs 16x1366) is 1.00x — exact break-even — while the MEAN of per-site ratios is 1.30x and the MEDIAN is 1.21x. The mean-of-ratios is biased upward because a site where structure is 3x cheaper contributes as much as one where it is 2x more expensive, despite costing a fraction of the tokens. The ratio of totals is the number to quote for 'what does a browsing session cost'; the median is the number to quote for 'what does a typical page cost'. Neither is the 3.49x measured on the synthetic duel pages. Structure wins on 10/16 sites. The reason is structural and worth stating plainly in any paper: a screenshot has a FLAT cost that depends only on the viewport, while a structured view scales with information density. So the ratio is not a property of the method, it is a property of the page. Range 0.47x (Hacker News: 2917 tokens of pure text, the structured view costs TWICE a screenshot) to 3.11x (Vercel: 439 tokens, a sparse marketing page). By category: vitrine 2.20x, webapp-canvas 1.75x, presse 1.21x, reference 1.11x, media 0.97x, commerce 0.82x, webapp 0.80x. Structure wins on visually rich / semantically sparse pages and LOSES on text-dense ones — which is the opposite of the intuition that 'text is cheap'. Two corrections in favour of the structured side, both real: (a) a viewport screenshot only shows one screen, and covering a whole page took 7.6 screens on average (19 on Stripe and Amazon), so the whole-page comparison is 1.31x with the naive whole-document view and much better if the router only ever needs one screen; (b) at Retina 2x the screenshot costs 4784 tokens on a high-res model, moving the average ratio to 4.54x — but only 1534 on a legacy-tier model (1.46x), because the API downscales before charging. 6/16 sites raised a consent banner (Stripe, Vercel, YouTube, BBC, Amazon.fr, leboncoin), which a router must dismiss before the view means anything — it is the single most common real-web obstacle we hit, ahead of any rendering issue.

measurements.notes: COST OF THE WHOLE SESSION: 16826 structured tokens across 9 view reads vs 12294 tokens if the same 9 looks had been screenshots at CSS resolution — the structured route is 1.37x MORE expensive here, and that is the honest number to publish. It flips to 3.5x cheaper if the screenshots are Retina 2x on a high-res model (4784 each). SCROLL-AND-SEARCH, measured: the 'More' link on Hacker News is below the fold, so the router read the view, failed to find the target, scrolled 90% of a viewport, and read again — 2 views for 1 target. Both channels pay this equally (a screenshot shows one screen too), so scrolling does not favour either side; what it does is make the AVERAGE cost of finding a target a function of where the target sits, which no single-screenshot benchmark captures. FIRST ROUND SCORED 3/6 AND ALL THREE FAILURES WERE THE ROUTER'S, NOT THE CHANNEL'S — this is the most useful result in the cell, so it is recorded rather than quietly fixed. (i) The router matched text lines and ignored the interactive line whose box contained them, so it aimed at MDN's 'Tutorial' assuming a link; the view had already published 'summary 16,409,224,32' on the line immediately above. The click was CORRECT — it toggled the disclosure widget, screenshot-confirmed collapsed — only the expectation was wrong. Reading the affordance off the joined control fixed it. (ii) The router expected a 'Pull requests' tab on torvalds/linux, a repo that has PRs disabled. The view did not offer one, and the screenshot confirms the tab genuinely does not exist. That is the desired failure mode — an explicit 'not found' rather than a plausible-looking click — so it is now a first-class negative-control step. (iii) A wrong URL regex. The lesson generalises past this probe: when a semantic router misfires, the first hypothesis should be that it under-used the view, not that the view lied. Here the view was complete in all three cases.
